issues.legal_issue: A conviction for a terrorist act cannot stand when the prosecution has neither alleged nor proved the statutory ingredients of that offence.
material_facts: The appellants were convicted under the provision concerning terrorist acts, but the prosecution evidence did not establish its ingredients.
The trial court gave no discussion explaining how the provision applied to the evidence.
The State conceded on appeal that the conviction under that provision was not made out.
issues.conclusion: The convictions and sentences for the terrorist-act offence were set aside, and the appellants were acquitted of that charge.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied Section 3 of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, and held that a trial court must examine whether the prosecution evidence establishes the ingredients of the charged offence; the fact that the investigating agency charged the offence does not justify a mechanical conviction. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_from_criminal_conviction: The case is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.terrorist_offence_ingredients_not_allege: The prosecution neither alleges nor establishes facts satisfying the required ingredients of the terrorist offence.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction appeal concerns a terrorist offence and the required ingredients were neither alleged nor proved, the conviction for that offence is set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A later accused's statement that repeats information already given and leading to discovery of the same fact is not admissible as a discovery statement.
material_facts: One accused first disclosed where the concealed body was located and said he could point out the place and have it recovered.
The body was recovered after that first disclosure.
Two other accused later made statements about the same concealed body and the same place.
The investigating officer acknowledged that the first disclosure was made before the other two.
issues.conclusion: The later statements were inadmissible because they could only lead to rediscovery of a fact already disclosed and capable of discovery.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, only the part of an accused's statement that distinctly leads to discovery of a fact is admissible. Once the fact has been discovered, Section 27 cannot be used again to rediscover it through another statement. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The statement is offered as evidence in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.prior_disclosure_led_to_discovery: An earlier accused's disclosure led to discovery of the relevant fact.
predicates.later_statement_repeats_same_discoverabl: A later accused's statement concerns the same fact that had already been disclosed and discovered.

issues.definition: In a criminal proceeding, when an earlier disclosure has led to discovery and a later statement repeats the same discoverable fact, the later statement is inadmissible.

issues.legal_issue: Recovery of a victim's body from a residence, without other evidence connecting the residents to the crime or showing their knowledge, does not establish their guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The only circumstance relied on against two residents was recovery of the victim's body from their home.
The prosecution's allegation that they wanted the tenant's family evicted and had instigated the crime was unsupported by evidence.
There was no evidence that the residents knew the body had been concealed in the room or that the crime had been committed at their instance.
issues.conclusion: The circumstantial evidence against the two residents was insufficient, their convictions and sentences were set aside, and they were acquitted.
issues.legal_principle: A criminal conviction cannot be founded on conjecture or surmise; circumstantial evidence must establish the accused's connection with the crime beyond reasonable doubt. The court applied the circumstantial-evidence standard and referred to the Indian Penal Code provisions under which the residents had been convicted, including Sections 120B and 302 read with Section 149. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_from_criminal_conviction: The case is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.body_recovered_from_residence: The victim's body was recovered from a residence occupied by the accused.
predicates.no_independent_evidence_of_residents_kno: No reliable evidence beyond the recovery connects the residents to the crime or establishes their knowledge of the concealment.

issues.definition: When a conviction appeal rests on recovery of a victim's body from the accused's residence but no independent evidence connects the residents to the crime or shows their knowledge, the residents are acquitted for insufficient evidence.

issues.legal_issue: An accused cannot be convicted on the basis of an inadmissible repeated disclosure when no other circumstance connects that accused with the crime.
material_facts: The accused's only alleged link to the crime was a disclosure statement made after another accused had already disclosed the location of the concealed body.
The later statement was inadmissible because it repeated information already disclosed and capable of discovery.
The prosecution relied on no other circumstance connecting this accused with the crime.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution had not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, and the accused's conviction and sentence were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, admits only the portion of a statement that distinctly leads to discovery; a repeated disclosure after the fact is already discovered is inadmissible. Without admissible evidence connecting the accused to the offence, the prosecution has not proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.only_link_is_inadmissible_repeated_discl: The sole circumstance connecting the accused to the crime is a statement that repeats a fact already disclosed and discovered.

issues.definition: When an accused's conviction appeal depends only on an inadmissible repeated disclosure, the accused is acquitted for insufficient evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A specimen writing obtained under a direction by a judicial officer who is not conducting an inquiry or trial cannot be used as a comparison specimen under the court's handwriting-comparison power.
material_facts: A specimen writing was taken from an accused under the direction of an executive magistrate.
No inquiry or trial was pending before that magistrate; the inquiry and trial were pending before the designated trial court.
The specimen was obtained during the investigation for comparison with disputed writings, and the expert's opinion relied on it.
issues.conclusion: The direction to provide the specimen writing was unauthorized, and neither the specimen nor the expert report based on it could be used against the accused.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 73 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the power to direct a person to provide a specimen writing is for enabling the court to compare writings in a proceeding before it. The court held that the power may be exercised by a court conducting an inquiry under the Code of Criminal Procedure or by the trial court, but not by a court or magistrate with no pending inquiry or trial and not merely to assist investigation. Sections 45 and 47 recognize other methods of proving handwriting, while Section 73 concerns comparison by the court, with expert assistance where appropriate. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.criminal_handwriting_comparison: A specimen writing is obtained for comparison with disputed writing in a criminal case.
predicates.specimen_ordered_by_officer_not_conducti: The person directing the specimen to be taken is not conducting an inquiry or trial in which the comparison is required.

issues.definition: When a specimen is obtained for criminal handwriting comparison at the direction of an officer who is not conducting the relevant inquiry or trial, the specimen and the resulting expert opinion are unusable.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution must establish the authorship of disputed letters through admissible evidence before relying on them to connect an accused with a crime.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on two ransom letters and an expert opinion comparing them with the accused's specimen writing.
The specimen had been obtained under an unauthorized direction and could not be used for the comparison.
The victim's mother testified that the letters produced at trial were not the letters she had found, and the prosecution did not explain how the produced letters came to be before the police.
After the letters were excluded as evidence of the accused's authorship, no other circumstance connected the accused with the crime.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution failed to establish that the accused wrote the letters or to prove the case against him beyond reasonable doubt; his conviction and sentence were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Handwriting may be proved by admission, a witness who saw it written, expert opinion under Section 45 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, evidence of a person acquainted with the handwriting under Section 47, or comparison under Section 73. The comparison opinion must rest on a specimen lawfully obtained, and the court must assess the evidence and its basis. The prosecution must prove the disputed writing's authorship beyond reasonable doubt before it can be used to connect an accused to a crime. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.disputed_letters_are_not_proved_as_accus: The prosecution fails to establish through admissible evidence that the accused authored the disputed letters.
predicates.no_other_linking_evidence: No other evidence connects the accused with the crime once the letters are not relied on.

issues.definition: When disputed letters are not proved to be the accused's writing and no other evidence connects the accused to the crime, the accused is acquitted for failure to prove authorship and guilt.

issues.legal_issue: A murder conviction may be sustained on circumstantial evidence when the circumstances are firmly established and form a complete chain excluding a reasonable hypothesis of innocence.
material_facts: A witness saw the accused in a perplexed state on the day the child disappeared, and that evidence was not challenged in cross-examination.
The accused voluntarily made the first disclosure identifying where the concealed body could be recovered.
The accused led the police to the indicated room and pointed out the place where the body was recovered from beneath a heap of chaff.
The testimony about the disclosure and recovery was cogent, trustworthy, and not undermined in cross-examination.
The medical evidence supported the prosecution case.
issues.conclusion: The circumstantial chain established the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt; his conviction for murder and life sentence were maintained, while his separate conspiracy conviction was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the rule for circumstantial evidence that the established circumstances must form a complete chain, point unerringly to guilt, and exclude hypotheses consistent with innocence. Under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the portion of the accused's voluntary disclosure that led to discovery of the concealed body was admissible. The murder conviction was maintained under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_from_murder_conviction: The case is an appeal challenging a conviction for murder.
predicates.voluntary_first_disclosure_led_to_body_r: The accused voluntarily made the first disclosure of the body's location and led the police to its recovery.
predicates.circumstances_form_complete_chain_exclud: The proved circumstances, considered together, point to the accused's guilt and exclude a reasonable hypothesis of innocence.

issues.definition: When a murder conviction appeal involves a voluntary first disclosure leading to recovery of the body and the proved circumstances form a complete chain excluding innocence, the murder conviction is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A conspiracy conviction cannot stand when the evidence does not establish an agreement or a reliable connection between the accused and the alleged conspirators.
material_facts: The alleged conspiracy involving the accused and other family members was based on an unsupported claim that they wanted a tenant's family evicted and had instigated the crime.
The witnesses to the alleged extra-judicial account turned hostile, and no reliance was placed on that account.
The prosecution led no evidence establishing a connection between the accused and the other alleged participants.
issues.conclusion: The conspiracy conviction was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code provides for punishment of criminal conspiracy; the court held on the evidence that the alleged agreement and connection among the accused had not been established. Mere conjecture or an unsupported inference cannot sustain a conspiracy conviction. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_from_conspiracy_conviction: The case is an appeal challenging a conviction for criminal conspiracy.
predicates.no_reliable_evidence_of_agreement_or_con: The prosecution presents no reliable evidence establishing an agreement to commit the crime or a connection between the accused and the alleged participants.

issues.definition: When a conspiracy conviction appeal has no reliable evidence establishing an agreement or connection among the alleged participants, the conspiracy conviction is set aside.
